section_title: What did God call His rescued people to become?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 In the third month, on the same day of the month that the Israelites had left the land of Egypt, they came to the Wilderness of Sinai. 2 After they had set out from Rephidim, they entered the Wilderness of Sinai, and Israel camped there in front of the mountain. 3 Then Moses went up to God, and the LORD called to him from the mountain, “This is what you are to tell the house of Jacob and explain to the sons of Israel: 4 ‘You have seen for yourselves what I did to Egypt, and how I carried you on eagles’ wings and brought you to Myself. 5 Now if you will indeed obey My voice and keep My covenant, you will be My treasured possession out of all the nations—for the whole earth is Mine. 6 And unto Me you shall be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.’ These are the words that you are to speak to the Israelites.”

7 So Moses went back and summoned the elders of the people and set before them all these words that the LORD had commanded him. 8 And all the people answered together, “We will do everything that the LORD has spoken.” So Moses brought their words back to the LORD. 9 The LORD said to Moses, “Behold, I will come to you in a dense cloud, so that the people will hear when I speak with you, and they will always put their trust in you.” And Moses relayed to the LORD what the people had said.

10 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Go to the people and consecrate them today and tomorrow. They must wash their clothes 11 and be prepared by the third day, for on the third day the LORD will come down on Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people. 12 And you are to set up a boundary for the people around the mountain and tell them, ‘Be careful not to go up on the mountain or touch its base. Whoever touches the mountain shall surely be put to death. 13 No hand shall touch him, but he shall surely be stoned or shot with arrows—whether man or beast, he must not live.’ Only when the ram’s horn sounds a long blast may they approach the mountain.” 14 When Moses came down from the mountain to the people, he consecrated them, and they washed their clothes. 15 “Be prepared for the third day,” he said to the people. “Do not draw near to a woman.”

context_lines: Israel arrives in the Wilderness of Sinai in the third month after leaving Egypt and camps before the mountain. God’s first message recalls what He has already done: He defeated Egypt, carried the people on eagles’ wings and brought them to Himself. The call to obey follows His rescue and care.

God promises that, if they obey His voice and keep His covenant, the binding agreement He gives them, they will be His treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. The Hebrew word סְגֻלָּה, *segullah* (seh-gooh-LAH), means a valued possession or treasure, as [Brown–Driver–Briggs](https://biblehub.com/hebrew/5459.htm) explains. The whole earth belongs to God; Israel is being set apart within it to belong to Him and serve Him.

Moses brings the message to the elders, and the people agree to do what the LORD has spoken. God then promises to speak with Moses in a dense cloud so the people can hear and continue to trust him as the one bringing God’s words to them.

The coming meeting requires preparation. The people are to wash their clothes, refrain from sexual relations for the appointed time and respect a boundary around the mountain. God gives both an invitation to meet Him and instructions for how they may approach. The preparations make clear that this is a meeting with the holy God who has called them.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-moses-called-exodus/) understands the covenant as a gracious invitation to belong to God and serve Him. He reads the kingdom of priests as the whole nation being brought near and devoted to God’s service. Christian traditions differ in how they relate this covenant and its law to life under Christ.

The Reformed [Westminster Confession, 7.5–6](https://www.opc.org/wcf.html), understands the time of the law and the time of the gospel as two forms of one saving covenant. Before Christ came, promises, sacrifices and other observances pointed people toward Him; after His coming, the same grace is made known more fully.

The Catholic Church’s [Catechism, 1961–1964](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_three/section_one/chapter_three/article_1/ii_the_old_law.index.html), describes the law given to Israel as preparation for Christ. It teaches what is good and exposes sin, while the law itself does not supply the Spirit’s power to fulfill it.

A different account appears in [Dallas Theological Seminary’s statement, article V](https://www.dts.edu/about/doctrinal-statement/). It treats the law, the church and the future kingdom as distinct stages in which God gives people different responsibilities. It explicitly teaches salvation by grace through faith in every period. This is the institution’s stated reading, not a claim that all evangelical churches agree with it.
god_plan_lines: [1 Peter 2:4–12](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_peter/2.htm) takes up the language of a royal priesthood, holy nation and people belonging to God when addressing believers in Christ. Their calling includes declaring His goodness and living honorably so that others may glorify Him. Being set apart carries a purpose for how His people live and bear witness.

[Revelation 1:4–6](https://biblehub.com/bsb/revelation/1.htm) connects this calling with Jesus’ saving work: He loves His people, frees them from their sins by His blood and makes them a kingdom and priests to His God and Father. The purpose of rescue includes service and worship.

[Galatians 3:15–29](https://biblehub.com/bsb/galatians/3.htm) explains that the later law does not cancel God’s earlier promise to Abraham. It leads the discussion toward Christ and the inheritance received through faith. The covenant at Sinai is part of the story through which Scripture explains God’s promise, human sin and the coming of Christ.
